Protections vary by country, so check the law. Ethical dilemmas include loyalty versus harm to users, and disclosure timing. Ask who may be harmed and whether less harmful options exist.

keyPoints: Computer misuse laws punish unauthorised access and interference, and each country defines its own offences.
Nigeria’s Cybercrimes Act 2015, the UK Computer Misuse Act 1990 and the US CFAA 1986 are national examples.
Authorisation and scope are central, but permission does not settle every ethical question.
Professional codes require honesty, competence, confidentiality and avoidance of harm.
Responsible disclosure reports a vulnerability privately and allows time to fix it before publication.
Whistleblowing protections and duties vary by country, so check the law and seek advice.

en.title: Privacy and data protection
en.short: Personal data, privacy principles, consent, data minimisation and anonymisation under GDPR and Nigeria’s 2023 Act.

sections.heading: Personal data and privacy
sections.text:
Personal data is information about a person who is identified or can be identified. A name, phone number, location or online identifier can be personal data. Privacy is the wider idea of control over one’s information and freedom from intrusion. Data protection is the set of rules for handling personal data.

Processing means any use of personal data, such as collecting, storing or sharing it. The EU General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) applies in the EU and EEA. Nigeria’s Data Protection Act 2023 applies in Nigeria. Other countries have their own laws, so check the current official source.

sections.heading: Principles and consent
sections.text:
Common principles include lawfulness, fairness and transparency; purpose limitation; data minimisation; accuracy; storage limitation; security; and accountability. Purpose limitation means using data only for stated, legitimate purposes. Data minimisation means collecting only what is adequate, relevant and necessary.

Consent is one lawful basis for processing. Under the GDPR it must be freely given, specific, informed and unambiguous, shown by a clear affirmative act, and easy to withdraw. Nigeria’s Act also recognises consent and similar principles. Example: Ada’s Enugu store asks for date of birth and gender at checkout. Delivery needs an address and phone number, so remove the extra fields. A newsletter box must be separate and unticked.

sections.heading: Anonymisation
sections.text:
Anonymisation means processing personal data so that no person can be identified by any reasonably likely means. Anonymised data is generally outside data protection law, because it is no longer personal data. Pseudonymisation replaces identifiers with codes. It lowers risk but is not anonymisation, because a key can re-identify people.

Removing names alone is often not enough. Phone numbers or rare details can still identify someone. Example: a clinic in a small town deletes names from a table of three patients with a rare condition. If the town and ages remain, readers may still know who they are. It should aggregate or suppress small groups. Rules differ by country, so check current guidance.

keyPoints: Personal data is any information that identifies or can identify a living person.
Data protection principles include lawfulness, fairness, transparency, purpose limitation, data minimisation, accuracy, storage limitation, security and accountability.
Consent must be freely given, specific, informed and unambiguous, and can be withdrawn.
Data minimisation means collecting only adequate, relevant and necessary data.
Anonymised data is generally outside data protection law, but pseudonymised data remains personal data.
The GDPR and Nigeria’s Data Protection Act 2023 share ideas but differ in detail; check the law that applies.

en.title: Advanced cryptography and post-quantum security
en.short: Provable security, pairings, zero-knowledge, MPC, and the quantum threat to public-key cryptography.

sections.heading: Provable security
sections.text: Provable security relates a scheme to a hard problem. A reduction shows that any attacker who breaks the scheme can solve the hard problem, so the scheme is at least as hard to break. Proofs use security models such as IND-CPA and IND-CCA for encryption and EUF-CMA for signatures. They may rely on idealised assumptions, notably the random oracle model, so a proof is evidence, not a guarantee about deployed code. A proof does not remove implementation risk. Security definitions fix what an attacker may do.

sections.heading: Pairings and proofs
sections.text: An elliptic-curve pairing is a bilinear map e: G1 × G2 → GT between groups. Bilinear means e(aP, bQ) = e(P,Q)^(ab). If e(P,Q)=g, then e(2P,3Q)=g^6. Pairings support identity-based encryption, short signatures and some zero-knowledge systems. A zero-knowledge proof lets a prover convince a verifier that a statement is true without revealing anything beyond the truth of the statement. It needs completeness, soundness and zero-knowledge. zk-SNARKs are succinct non-interactive arguments of knowledge; some need a trusted setup.

sections.heading: Secure multiparty computation
sections.text: Secure multiparty computation (MPC) lets parties compute a joint function while keeping inputs private. Secret sharing, garbled circuits and oblivious transfer are common tools. Security is proved in a model: semi-honest parties follow the protocol; malicious parties may deviate. MPC is used in auctions, private statistics and key management.

sections.heading: Quantum threat and PQC
sections.text: Shor’s algorithm would break RSA, finite-field Diffie-Hellman and elliptic-curve discrete-log schemes on a large quantum computer. Grover’s algorithm gives a quadratic speed-up for search, so symmetric keys need larger sizes. Post-quantum cryptography uses problems believed hard for quantum computers: lattices, hashes, codes, multivariate equations and isogenies. The US NIST has standardised ML-KEM, ML-DSA and SLH-DSA. Hybrid schemes combine classical and post-quantum methods during migration.

keyPoints: A security reduction shows that breaking a scheme implies solving a believed-hard problem.
Pairings are bilinear: e(aP,bQ)=e(P,Q)^(ab).
Zero-knowledge proofs need completeness, soundness and zero-knowledge.
MPC keeps inputs private; semi-honest and malicious models give different guarantees.
Shor’s algorithm breaks RSA and elliptic-curve discrete log, while Grover’s algorithm gives a quadratic search speed-up.
Post-quantum families include lattice, hash, code, multivariate and isogeny; US NIST standards include ML-KEM, ML-DSA and SLH-DSA.

en.title: Research methods in cyber security
en.short: Designing, measuring, reproducing and ethically reporting cyber security research.

sections.heading: Design and literature
sections.text:
A research design is the plan that links a question to evidence. Start with a question that can be answered: descriptive, comparative or causal.

A literature review is a systematic search and critical summary of prior work; it shows the gap and prevents repeating known results. Record search terms, databases and inclusion rules so the review can be checked. Scope the question so it is feasible in the time available.

sections.heading: Threat modelling experiments
sections.text:
Threat modelling here means stating the adversary, assets, capabilities and assumptions that define the experimental setting. Define the attacker model (for example, a remote unauthenticated attacker), the system under test, and what counts as success.

This keeps claims honest: a result holds only under the stated model. Case: a study of a phishing detector should state whether it faces opportunistic or targeted attackers, and which email features are visible.

sections.heading: Measurement and evaluation
sections.text:
Operationalise variables: turn abstract ideas into measurable quantities. Use baselines, controls and repeated runs. Report precision and recall, not only accuracy, when classes are unbalanced.

Worked example: a detector flags 200 of 10,000 events; 50 are real attacks. Precision = 50 ÷ 200 = 0.25 (25%). Recall needs the total number of attacks, say 100: recall = 50 ÷ 100 = 0.50. Accuracy would mislead because most events are benign.

sections.heading: Reproducibility and ethics
sections.text:
Reproducibility means another researcher can obtain the same result from the same data, code and description. Share artefacts where law and consent allow; otherwise document them.

Ethics: seek approval from your institution’s ethics committee, protect participants and data, minimise harm, and follow responsible disclosure for vulnerabilities, which means reporting them to the vendor and allowing time for a fix before publishing details. Declare conflicts and funding. Never test on systems without permission.

keyPoints: Scope the research question so it is answerable with the time and data available.
A literature review is a documented, systematic search, not a casual reading list.
State the threat model and attacker assumptions; results hold only under them.
Use baselines and controls, and report precision and recall when classes are unbalanced.
Precision = true positives ÷ predicted positives; recall = true positives ÷ actual positives.
Reproducibility requires sharing or documenting data, code and method; obtain ethics approval and never test systems without permission.

en.title: Advanced systems security: trusted computing and side channels
en.short: TPMs, secure enclaves, formal verification and side-channel attacks, with their assumptions and limits.

sections.heading: Trusted platform modules
sections.text: A trusted platform module (TPM) is a chip, or firmware component, that stores keys and records measurements. During measured boot, each boot stage hashes the next stage and writes the hash into a platform configuration register (PCR). Remote attestation lets a server check those PCR values: the TPM signs a quote with a restricted key, so the server learns which software started. The trust anchor (the component you must trust) is the TPM vendor and the firmware that drives it. If that firmware is flawed, the measurements can be wrong.

sections.heading: Secure enclaves
sections.text: A secure enclave is an isolated execution area inside a processor. Intel SGX, AMD SEV and ARM TrustZone are examples; their details differ, so check the vendor documentation. Code and data inside an enclave are protected from the operating system and hypervisor. The processor and its microcode (low-level firmware) become the trust anchor. Enclaves reduce the trusted computing base (the components that must be trusted) but do not remove it. They also share hardware resources, which opens side channels.

sections.heading: Side channels
sections.text: A side-channel attack learns secrets from implementation behaviour rather than from the algorithm. Timing, cache access, power draw and electromagnetic emission are common channels. Example: if a program indexes a table with a secret key, an attacker who measures which cache line is loaded can infer key bits. Defences include constant-time code, cache partitioning and speculation barriers. Each defence assumes a threat model; a defence against remote timing may not stop a local power attack.

sections.heading: Verification and limits
sections.text: Formal verification proves that a model meets a specification. The seL4 microkernel is a well-known verified system, but its proof assumes correct hardware, boot code and specification. Current research applies verification to crypto code and enclave monitors. To evaluate a defence, ask what is trusted, what is modelled, and what is excluded. A proof or TPM quote is only as strong as its assumptions. Hardware bugs and side channels often sit outside those assumptions.

keyPoints: A TPM stores keys and records boot measurements in PCRs; remote attestation signs those values for a verifier.
Secure enclaves isolate code inside the CPU, but the CPU, microcode and shared hardware remain trusted.
Side channels leak secrets through timing, cache, power or electromagnetic behaviour, not through the algorithm.
Constant-time code, cache partitioning and speculation barriers are defences, each with its own threat model.
Formal verification proves a model against a specification; it does not prove the hardware or the assumptions.
Evaluate any defence by naming its trust anchor, threat model and excluded attacks.
